history.heading: The Swazi kingdom
paragraphs: Eswatini, a small landlocked kingdom between South Africa and Mozambique, takes its name from the Swazi people. In the 18th and 19th centuries, kings such as Sobhuza I and Mswati II united clans into a strong state, which became known for its military strength.
Under pressure from Boer and British settlers, Swazi kings granted extensive land and mineral concessions in the late 19th century.

history.heading: British protectorate and independence
paragraphs: Swaziland was administered by the South African Republic and then became a British protectorate after the Boer War. It gained independence on 6 September 1968 under King Sobhuza II, who reigned for 82 years, one of the longest reigns in history. In 1973 he abolished the constitution and banned political parties.
King Mswati III has reigned since 1986. In 2018 he changed the country's name from Swaziland to Eswatini. Pro-democracy protests in 2021 were violently suppressed.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: SiSwati and English are official languages. Most people are Christian, often combined with traditional beliefs. Traditional ceremonies remain central: the Umhlanga (Reed Dance), in which thousands of young women present reeds to the queen mother, and the Incwala, a sacred kingship ceremony.
Traditional dress, music and dance are widely practised, and the monarchy plays a central role in cultural identity.

politics.heading: Absolute monarchy
paragraphs: Eswatini is Africa's last absolute monarchy. The king appoints the prime minister and some members of parliament, and can veto legislation. Political parties cannot contest elections; candidates stand as individuals through the tinkhundla system of local constituencies.
Pro-democracy groups call for multiparty democracy and limits on royal power.

economy.heading: Sugar and links with South Africa
paragraphs: The economy is closely tied to South Africa, the main trading partner and source of imports. Sugar, soft drink concentrates, wood pulp and textiles are key exports. Most people depend on subsistence agriculture.

The lilangeni is pegged to the South African rand, which is also legal tender. Eswatini has high inequality and unemployment, and one of the world's highest HIV rates, though treatment has greatly improved.
